title: Should we go to the birds for teachers?
source_text: Ἐχρῆν οὖν τὸν Κέλσον, διὰ τῶν προκειμένων βουλόμενον θειότερα καὶ σοφώτερα ἀποδεῖξαι τὰ ἄλογα ζῷα τῶν ἀνθρώπων, κατασκευάσαι διὰ πλειόνων ὡς ὑπάρχουσαν τὴν τοιάνδε μαντικὴν καὶ τὴν ἀπολογίαν μετὰ τοῦτ᾿ ἐναργεστέρως ἀποδεῖξαι καὶ ἀποδεικτικῶς ἀποδοκιμάσαι μὲν τοὺς λόγους τῶν ἀναιρούντων τὰς τοιασδὶ μαντείας ἀποδεικτικῶς δ᾿ ἀνατρέψαι καὶ τοὺς λόγους τῶν εἰπόντων ἀπὸ δαιμόνων ἢ θεῶν γίνεσθαι τὰς κινήσεις τοῖς ζῴοις πρὸς τὸ μαντεύσασθαι καὶ μετὰ ταῦτα κατασκευάσαι περὶ τῆς τῶν ἀλόγων ζῴων ψυχῆς ὡς θειοτέρας. οὕτω γὰρ ἂν πρὸς τὰ πιθανὰ αὐτοῦ, ἐπιδειξαμένου φιλόσοφον περὶ τῶν τηλικούτων ἕξιν, κατὰ τὸ δυνατὸν ἡμῖν ἐνέστημεν· ἀνατρέποντες μὲν τὸ ὅτι σοφώτερα τὰ ἄλογα ζῷα τῶν ἀνθρώπων, ψευδοποιοῦντες δὲ καὶ ὅτι ἐννοίας ἔχει τοῦ θείου ἱερωτέρας ἡμῶν καὶ ὅτι ὁμιλίας ἔχει πρὸς ἄλληλα ἱεράς τινας. νυνὶ δ᾿ ὁ ἐγκαλῶν ἡμῖν ὅτι πιστεύομεν τῷ ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεῷ ἀξιοῖ ἡμᾶς πιστεύειν ὅτι αἱ ψυχαὶ τῶν ὀρνίθων θειοτέρας ἔχουσιν ἐννοίας καὶ τρανοτέρας ἀνθρώπων. ὅπερ εἰ ἀληθές ἐστιν. ὄρνιθες μᾶλλον τρανοτέρας Κέλσου ἔχουσι περὶ θεοῦ ἐννοίας· καὶ οὐ θαυμαστὸν εἰ Κέλσου. τοῦ ἐπὶ τοσοῦτον τὸν ἄνθρωπον ἐξευτελίζοντος. ἀλλὰ γὰρ ὅσον ἐπὶ Κέλσῳ οἱ ὄρνιθες μείζονας καὶ θειοτέρας ἔχουσιν ἐννοίας οὐ λέγω ἡμῶν Χριστιανῶν ἢ τῶν ταῖς αὐταῖς ἡμῖν γραφαῖς χρωμένων Ἰουδαίων ἀλλὰ γὰρ καὶ τῶν παρ᾿ Ἕλλησι θεολόγων· ἄνθρωποι γὰρ ἦσαν. μᾶλλον οὖν κατὰ Κέλσον κατείληφε τὴν τοῦ θείου φύσιν τὸ τῶν δῆθεν μαντικῶν ὀρνίθων γένος ἢ Φερεκύδης καὶ Πυθαγόρας καὶ Σωκράτης καὶ Πλάτων. καὶ ἐχρῆν γε ἡμᾶς πρὸς τοὺς ὄρνιθας φοιτᾶν διδασκάλους· ἵν᾿. ὥσπερ κατὰ τὴν Κέλσου ὑπόληψιν διδάσκουσιν ἡμᾶς μαντικῶς τὰ ἐσόμενα. οὕτω καὶ [περὶ] τοῦ ἀμφιβάλλειν περὶ τοῦ θείου ἀπαλλάξωσι τοὺς ἀνθρώπους. ἣν κατειλήφασι τρανὴν περὶ αὐτοῦ ἔννοιαν παραδιδόντες. Κέλσῳ μὲν οὖν ἀκολουθεῖ, τῷ διαφέρειν ἡγουμένῳ τῶν ἀνθρώπων τοὺς ὄρνιθας, διδασκάλοις αὐτὸν χρᾶσθαι ὄρνισι καὶ μηδενὶ οὕτως τῶν φιλοσοφησάντων παρ᾿ Ἕλλησιν·
pass_a_gloss: It was needful then for Celsus, wishing through the things set forth to prove (ἀποδεῖξαι) the irrational animals more divine (θειότερα) and wiser than men, to establish (κατασκευάσαι) through more [words] that such divination (μαντική) exists, and after this to show more vividly (ἐναργεστέρως) the defence (ἀπολογία), and demonstratively (ἀποδεικτικῶς) to reject (ἀποδοκιμάσαι) the arguments (λόγοι) of those abolishing (ἀναιρούντων) such divinations, and demonstratively to overturn (ἀνατρέψαι) also the arguments of those saying the movements come to the animals from demons (δαίμονες) or gods for prophesying, and after these to establish about the soul (ψυχή) of irrational animals as more divine. For so, against his plausibilities (πιθανά), he having displayed a philosophic habit (φιλόσοφος ἕξις) about such great matters, we would have stood against [them] (ἐνέστημεν) as far as possible for us: overturning that the irrational animals [are] wiser than men, and falsifying (ψευδοποιοῦντες) both that they have notions (ἔννοιαι) of the divine holier (ἱερωτέρας) than ours and that they have some holy converses (ὁμιλίαι) with one another. But now he who accuses (ἐγκαλῶν) us that we believe (πιστεύομεν) in the God over all (τῷ ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεῷ) thinks fit (ἀξιοῖ) that we believe that the souls of birds have more divine and clearer (τρανοτέρας) notions than men. Which if it is true, birds have clearer notions about God than Celsus; and no wonder if than Celsus, who so far cheapens (ἐξευτελίζοντος) man. But indeed as far as concerns Celsus, birds have greater and more divine notions, I do not say than us Christians or than the Jews using the same Scriptures (γραφαί) as us, but even than the theologians (θεολόγοι) among the Greeks; for they were men. Rather then according to Celsus the race of the supposedly (δῆθεν) prophetic birds has grasped (κατείληφε) the nature of the divine than Pherecydes and Pythagoras and Socrates and Plato. And it was needful for us to resort (φοιτᾶν) to birds as teachers (διδάσκαλοι), so that, just as according to Celsus' supposition (ὑπόληψις) they teach us prophetically (μαντικῶς) the things to come, so also they might free (ἀπαλλάξωσι) men from doubting (ἀμφιβάλλειν) about the divine, handing on (παραδιδόντες) the clear notion they have grasped about it. It follows (ἀκολουθεῖ) then for Celsus, who thinks birds to excel (διαφέρειν) men, to use birds as teachers and none thus of those who philosophized among Greeks.
pass_b_english: Celsus, then, since by these arguments he wished to prove the irrational animals more divine and wiser than men, ought to have established at greater length that such divination exists. After that he ought to have set out its defence more clearly, rejecting with proof the arguments of those who do away with such divinations, and overturning with proof as well the arguments of those who said that the animals’ movements for prophesying come from demons or gods. And after that he ought to have established that the soul of the irrational animals is more divine. Had he done so, and shown a philosopher’s habit of mind on matters so great, we would have opposed his plausible arguments as far as we were able: overturning the claim that the irrational animals are wiser than men, and proving false the claims that they have holier notions of the divine than ours and that they hold some holy converse with one another.

As it is, the man who reproaches us for believing in the God who is over all expects us to believe that the souls of birds have more divine and clearer notions than men. If this is true, birds have clearer notions about God than Celsus has; and it is no wonder that they surpass Celsus, who belittles man to such a degree. But indeed, so far as Celsus is concerned, birds have greater and more divine notions, I do not say than we Christians, or than the Jews who use the same Scriptures as we do, but even than the theologians among the Greeks; for they were men. According to Celsus, then, the race of supposedly prophetic birds has grasped the nature of the divine better than Pherecydes and Pythagoras and Socrates and Plato. Then we ought indeed to go to the birds as our teachers, so that, just as on Celsus’s view they teach us by divination what is to come, so too they may free men from doubting about the divine, by handing on the clear notion of it they have grasped. It follows, then, for Celsus, who thinks birds superior to men, that he should use birds as his teachers, and none of those who have pursued philosophy among the Greeks.

choices.choice: 'by demonstration to reject ... by demonstration to overturn' to 'rejecting with proof ... overturning with proof' (ἀποδεικτικῶς kept, stiff order removed)
'movements for prophesying are produced by demons or gods' to 'come from demons or gods' (ἀπὸ ... γίνεσθαι)
'notions of the divine holier than ours' to 'holier notions of the divine than ours' (natural order)
ἀξιοῖ: 'asks us to believe' to 'expects us to believe'
'and no wonder, if clearer than Celsus' (elliptical) to 'and it is no wonder that they surpass Celsus, who belittles man to such a degree'
'And we ought to go' to 'Then we ought indeed to go' (keeps the ironic γε)

The God “who is over all” (ὁ ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεός) is capitalised. Origen recalls Celsus’s charge (earlier in the work) that Christians believe without reasoning; kept as “reproaches us for believing”. ἀξιοῖ rendered “expects” (demands as his due). οὐ λέγω … ἀλλὰ γὰρ καὶ rendered “I do not say than … but even than”. ἐχρῆν γε ἡμᾶς … φοιτᾶν is ironic (“Then we ought indeed to go”). οὕτω καὶ [περὶ] τοῦ ἀμφιβάλλειν: Koetschau brackets περὶ; not translated. μηδενὶ οὕτως: οὕτως taken loosely with the conclusion (“and none of those”), not rendered separately. Pherecydes of Syros is named as an early Greek theologian alongside Pythagoras, Socrates and Plato; no classical quotation here. No Scripture in this chapter.
